– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

Diagnosis:
The failing test `testGetLineNumberWithCR()` is designed to check the line number counting when the input uses CR (`'\r'`) as the line separator. The test creates a CSVParser with a `CSVFormat` specifying the line separator as `'\r'`. The test then asserts that after parsing the first record, the line number reported should be 1.

The call chain for `getLineNumber()` in `CSVParser` forwards the call to `lexer.getLineNumber()` and then further to `in.getLineNumber()`, where `in` is an instance of `ExtendedBufferedReader`. In `ExtendedBufferedReader`, the `getLineNumber()` method simply returns an internal `lineCounter`.

Looking at how the line counting is done in `ExtendedBufferedReader`, the `read()` and `read(char[], int, int)` methods increment `lineCounter` on encountering `'\n'`. The `read(char[], int, int)` method also increments `lineCounter` on encountering `'\r'`. This suggests it supports CR and LF properly for bulk reads. 

However, the `read()` method only increments on `'\n'`, not `'\r'`.

More importantly, the `readLine()` method overrides `BufferedReader.readLine()`, which correctly treats `\r`, `\n`, and `\r\n` as line terminators (dropping them). The `readLine()` method increments `lineCounter` blindly by 1 for every line returned, regardless of what the actual line separator was. It does not distinguish between CR or LF or CRLF. This behavior matches standard `BufferedReader.readLine()`.

The issue arises because `read()` and `read(char[])` increment line counters by detecting explicit newline characters, but `readLine()` increments the counter independently of what the separator actually was, i.e., by counting every call that returns a line. This causes inconsistency: code path using `readLine()` (like CSV parsing) may not correctly support CR-only line endings if other parts of the code rely on explicit checks for `'\n'`.

The current bug report confirms this as ExtendedBufferedReader treats line endings inconsistently. It suggests that ExtendedBufferedReader should increment the line counter also on detecting a CR character in `read()`, to support flexible line endings consistently, matching the behavior in `read(char[])` and `readLine()`.

The test fails because the CSVParser expects the line number to reflect the CR-separated lines. Because `read()` only increments on `\n` but not on `\r`, the line counting under CR separators is inconsistent depending on which read method is used, causing the test that expects line number 1 immediately to fail or give incorrect line numbers.

In summary:
- `ExtendedBufferedReader.read()` increments lineCounter only on `\n`, not on `\r`.
- `ExtendedBufferedReader.read(char[])` increments lineCounter on both `\n` and `\r`.
- `ExtendedBufferedReader.readLine()` blindly increments lineCounter on each line.
- The mix of these inconsistent treatments causes the line number counting to fail for CR line endings when the parser uses the `read()` method.
- The fix is to treat CR in `read()` consistently like in the bulk read method (`read(char[])`), so both handle all standard line endings identically.

Therefore, the root cause is the incomplete handling of CR character in the `ExtendedBufferedReader.read()` method for line counting. It should increment lineCounter on CR as well as LF, ensuring consistent line counting across all reading methods.

Recent bug reports are not relevant here as they deal with unrelated topics (MYSQL CSV format, remove method in iterator, immutability of CSVFormat).

This diagnosis explains why `testGetLineNumberWithCR()` fails and aligns with the current bug report about inconsistent handling of line endings in ExtendedBufferedReader.

Next, I'll suggest the methods to fix.
org.apache.commons.csv.ExtendedBufferedReader.read()
org.apache.commons.csv.ExtendedBufferedReader.readLine()

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
